Time complexity. Time complexity measures how the running time of an algorithm grows with the size of the input, typically expressed using Big O notation like O of n, O of n squared, or O of two to the n. It's the primary lens through which computer scientists classify algorithms and problems, enabling comparison of efficiency and defining major complexity classes like P and NP.

Big O notation provides an upper bound on running time. O of n is linear, O of n log n is linearithmic, O of n squared is quadratic, and O of two to the n is exponential. Time complexity measures the worst-case number of elementary operations—comparisons, arithmetic, and so on—as a function of input size n. The practical boundary is polynomial time, O of n to the k for some fixed k. Algorithms are considered efficient or feasible if they run in polynomial time. Exponential time—O of two to the n or worse—is prohibitive for large inputs. Many fundamental problems, including the Halting Problem and NP-complete problems, have no known polynomial-time algorithms.

Linear time O of n, logarithmic O of log n, and linearithmic O of n log n are all very efficient. Sorting via merge-sort achieves O of n log n, which is close to optimal for comparison-based sorting. The complexity class P contains problems solvable in polynomial time. NP contains problems verifiable in polynomial time. The famous open question is whether P equals NP. If they were equal, every problem we can verify quickly could be solved quickly, which would revolutionize cryptography and computation. The current consensus is that P does not equal NP, meaning there are problems whose solutions are easy to check but hard to find. Related to these is the concept of amortized analysis, which averages the cost of operations over many executions to give a more realistic picture than worst-case analysis alone.
